claims.text: The HTTP method is the first token of a request's start line and names the kind of action the client intends on the target address.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9112 §3 Request Line; RFC 9110 §9.1 Methods Overview

claims.text: The protocol defines what each method means, but the origin server is what implements it; a server can answer a GET destructively, and the specification's answer is a requirement on the resource owner, not a mechanism that stops it.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §9.1 Overview and §9.2.1 Safe Methods (the MUST on the resource owner, and the absence of enforcement)

claims.text: GET requests a transfer of the target resource's current representation and is a safe method, so it is not expected to change server state.
POST asks the target resource to process the enclosed representation according to that resource's own semantics, commonly creating a new resource.
PUT asks that the state of the target resource be created or replaced by the representation enclosed in the request.
PATCH is a method defined specifically for partial updates: it changes part of the target rather than replacing it whole.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §14.5 Partial PUT (PATCH named as the method defined for partial updates)

claims.text: DELETE asks the origin server to remove the association between the target resource and its current functionality.
A method is idempotent when the intended effect on the server of several identical requests with that method is the same as the effect of a single such request.

PUT, DELETE and the safe methods (GET among them) are idempotent; POST and PATCH are not on that list, so repeating either is not promised harmless (a PATCH that adds an item to an order adds a second one if sent twice).
Idempotency constrains the effect left on the server, not the status code returned; a repeated DELETE may answer differently while leaving the same end state.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §9.2.2 (idempotency applies to what was requested, not to the response)

claims.text: When a form (the fields on a page that its button sends) was submitted with POST, a browser usually asks the user to confirm before re-sending it when the resulting page is reloaded.
claims.source_hint: HTML Standard, navigation and reload of a document whose navigation used POST (form resubmission confirmation)

claims.text: A cache may store a GET response and reuse it for a later equivalent request without forwarding that request to the server, which fits GET being safe (no state change requested); responses to DELETE are not cacheable.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §9.2.1 Safe Methods; §9.2.3 Cacheable Methods; RFC 9111 §3 Storing Responses in Caches

claims.text: A client may automatically retry an idempotent request after a communication failure; it should not automatically retry a non-idempotent one such as POST unless told the request is safe to repeat, since it cannot know whether the first arrived, though some clients do retry a POST.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §9.2.2 (automatic retry of idempotent requests; SHOULD NOT for non-idempotent; clients might retry POST on a closed connection)

claims.text: 201 (Created) indicates that one or more new resources were created, and the primary one is identified by the Location header field when that field is present.

A 204 (No Content) response carries no message body; 404 (Not Found) says the server found nothing at the target address; for PUT, a 200 (OK) or 204 (No Content) indicates the request completed successfully.
claims.source_hint: RFC 9110 §15.3.5 204 No Content; §15.5.5 404 Not Found; §9.3.4 PUT (200/204 on successful completion)

claims.text: curl sends GET unless -X names another method; a -d body makes it POST without -X; -w prints its format with %{http_code} replaced by the status code; -sS hides progress, -o discards the body, -H adds a header (Content-Type names the body's format), -D writes the response headers.
claims.source_hint: curl manual page: -X/--request, -d/--data, -w/--write-out (%{http_code}), -s/-S, -o, -H, -D; confirmed by the captured run at stage-0; RFC 9110 §8.3 Content-Type

claims.text: At tag stage-0 Caddy listens on :8080 inside the lab box (the script's localhost:8080) and answers the order paths with fixed responses that do not read the request body; no application behind them saves what a request sends.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang Caddyfile at stage-0 (header comment, :8080 site, the order handlers' fixed respond bodies); scripts/http/methods.sh lines 4-7

claims.text: Running scripts/http/methods.sh at stage-0 prints 200, 201, 200, 200, 204 for GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE, then HTTP/1.1 201 Created with Location: /api/v1/orders/13, then the same order body twice.
Matching the method to the intended action is not a matter of style, on the condition that any intermediary or retrying client sits on the path.
claims.source_hint: author's conclusion from claims 12 and 13; condition stated in the text

beyond_scope: Names 201, 204 and the Location header in section 5 so the captured output can be read; their general meaning belongs to foundation.l1.http-status-codes.
Says in one sentence that a stored copy of a GET answer may be reused, needed for outline item 4; the mechanism belongs to foundation.l1.http-caching.
Names /api/v1/orders as the address POST is sent to in Đơn Hàng, presented as this lab's arrangement and not as a rule of the protocol; why an API is laid out that way is backend L1 resource design.
